Experiment:
1. **Audit and pre-registration.** Refit each calibration spring by OLS on both loading and unloading rows; retain \(k\) as an interval because the samples are not proven to be the installed springs. Recompute \(c_i,h_i,B_i,G_i\) from the two-rotor tables. Convert the 16 network_C events into order/interval constraints and enumerate six-edge four-rotor graphs by interval branch-and-bound to obtain the baseline equivalence class. Pre-register measurement resolution, equivalence margins, and falsification rules.

2. **Two-rotor kernel experiment.** Use a modular two-rotor bed with the same rotor/drive hardware, interchangeable parallel/crossed couplings, and in-situ spring calibration. Factorially vary topology, attachment distance \(\ell\) (e.g. 0, 1.58, 3.15, 4.73, 6.3 cm), other-rotor state, direction, and coupling stiffness; use randomized order and five repeats. Record drive and rotor angles continuously at several slow rates to verify quasistatic rate independence and to capture reversal rows. Estimate \(c,h,B,G\) and fit \(b,q\). Test whether parallel coupling requires \(q\neq0\) and an \(\ell\)-dependent \(G\), while crossed bias-only predicts \(G\approx0\) with no \(\ell\)-dependent width. Nonzero or \(\ell\)-dependent crossed \(G\) falsifies the bias-only alternative. Test \(B\propto\ell^2\) and dimensionless collapse across rotors. Pair_B’s single \(\ell\) is not used to claim a sweep.

3. **Blinded four-rotor validation.** Build a four-rotor surrogate with known topology hidden from the analyst, using the same components. Record full cycles and 16 ordered events, run the identifiability pipeline with Stage 2 kernels, and check whether the true graph lies in the recovered equivalence class. Then add release thresholds and one-edge interventions to measure how much the class shrinks. This validates kernel transfer and the inference procedure before applying it to C.

4. **Network_C measurements.** Treat connectivity, stops, attachment coordinates, and reversal amplitudes as unknown. Measure each rotor’s release threshold under all eight neighbour-state patterns and both directions (\(4\times8\times2\), five repeats), holding the other three rotors at stops. Then perform six non-destructive single-edge interventions—disconnect or change \(\ell\) of one coupling—and repeat thresholds and cycle recording. Record constant-amplitude cycles at 60/80/100% of the safe drive range, five cycles each, with three remounts and full traces. For P3, add a calibrated offset preload to one rotor and predict only its flip position until bifurcation; for P4, sweep amplitude and test order preservation.

5. **Analysis and endpoints.** Fit kernels only on two-rotor data; do not pool pair_A and pair_B. Predict C event order and threshold intervals held-out, using measured C drive stiffness/stops and dimensionless kernels. Report forced edges, unresolved edges, equivalence-class size/entropy before and after each added measurement. Falsify the minimal pairwise model if no graph in the original equivalence class passes the new constraints, if crossed \(G\) is significant and \(\ell\)-dependent, or if preload changes non-target rotor order before the predicted bifurcation.

Rationale:
The calibration rows are a null result: fitted slopes reproduce the nominal values and loading–unloading gaps are tiny, so constitutive spring hysteresis cannot explain the large threshold windows. Decomposing each window into centre and half-width separates additive bias from differential gain and makes the proposed lever-arm mechanism directly testable. Fitting \(b,q\) on two-rotor devices prevents unconstrained edge fitting in C, but pair_A and pair_B are distinct devices, so transfer must be dimensionless and anchored by in-situ calibration. The 16 C events lack timestamps, reversal rows, and unique tie ordering; therefore they constrain topology only as an equivalence class. Release thresholds add the missing window map, while one-edge interventions attribute effects to individual edges. Blinding, a ground-truth surrogate, full traces, and amplitude/preload sweeps protect against circular inference and turn P3–P4 into held-out predictions. The design is feasible with standard encoder, motorized-drive, and load-cell instrumentation and preserves unknown C apparatus facts rather than inventing them.
